title: Bored at Work? You May Be Feeling 'Rustout'
paragraphs: We hear a lot about burnout — when too much work and stress leave people feeling exhausted.
But what if the problem is the opposite? What if your job isn't challenging enough?

Psychologists have a name for this: "rustout." Just as metal may rust when it isn't used, workers can lose motivation when they don't have enough chances to use their real skills. It happens when work feels too repetitive, easy or meaningless.
A worker may even be extremely busy, but if all that work gives them few chances to use their abilities meaningfully, it can still lead to rustout.

Signs of rustout include difficulty concentrating, daydreaming, procrastinating and doing only the bare minimum. Over time, workers who aren't challenged enough may lose motivation and confidence. Research has also linked long-term boredom at work with problems such as anxiety and depression.
The problem is far from rare. Recent research cited by the American Psychological Association (APA) found that more than 40% of workers felt underchallenged, stuck and unable to grow.
The way some workplaces are organized may play a role. When responsibility and decision-making stay at the top, employees can be left with limited tasks and little room to take initiative.
And rustout can hurt organizations too, as disengaged employees put in less effort, affecting productivity, profitability and staff retention.

However, it can be hard for people to admit they might be feeling rustout. Employees may worry that complaining about how uninteresting their work is will make them look lazy — or simply lead to them being given even more boring tasks.
So what can employers do? Giving workers more freedom and variety, and opportunities to learn new skills, work with others and take on new challenges, can all help.
"If you don't give people opportunities to do interesting and challenging work, you never discover what they're capable of," organizational psychologist Sharon Parker told the APA.
